source: Geometry_ Euclid and Beyond.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Hilbert incidence axioms
statement: Through any two distinct points there is exactly one line; every line contains at least two points, and suitable noncollinearity and intersection axioms govern the plane.
conditions: Points and lines satisfy Hilbert incidence primitives.
conclusion: Incidence constructions are uniquely determined where the axioms apply.
typical_uses: Separate incidence conclusions from metric or order assumptions.
common_misuses: Assuming two arbitrary lines intersect in Euclidean or projective geometry without parallel hypotheses.
bridge_lemmas: Distinct lines share at most one point.
repair_templates: State the relevant incidence axiom before asserting existence or uniqueness.

source: Geometry_ Euclid and Beyond.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Betweenness axioms
statement: Betweenness on a line is constrained by symmetry, uniqueness of the middle point, and Pasch-type separation axioms.
conditions: A ternary betweenness relation on collinear points is given.
conclusion: Segments and rays have consistent order behavior needed for between-point arguments.
typical_uses: Justify segment decomposition and Pasch configurations.
common_misuses: Using diagram intuition instead of an order axiom.
bridge_lemmas: Exactly one of three distinct collinear points lies between the other two.
repair_templates: Invoke the appropriate betweenness axiom for the claimed separation.

source: Geometry_ Euclid and Beyond.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Side-angle-side congruence
statement: Two triangles with two corresponding sides equal and the included angle equal are congruent.
conditions: The two side equalities and included-angle equality are established.
conclusion: All corresponding sides and angles are equal.
typical_uses: Prove triangle congruence and derive perpendicular or bisector properties.
common_misuses: Using a non-included angle or omitting correspondence.
bridge_lemmas: Rigid motions preserve lengths and angles.
repair_templates: Identify the included angle and match vertices explicitly.

source: Geometry_ Euclid and Beyond.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Similarity of triangles
statement: Equality of two corresponding angles implies triangle similarity; corresponding side ratios are equal.
conditions: Two pairs of corresponding angles are equal.
conclusion: The third angles are equal and corresponding sides are proportional.
typical_uses: Establish proportionality, intercept theorems, and trigonometric identities.
common_misuses: Assuming side proportionality without matching correspondence.
repair_templates: Specify vertex correspondence before writing ratios.

source: Geometry_ Euclid and Beyond.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Pythagorean theorem
statement: In a right triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the legs.
conditions: ABC is a Euclidean right triangle with right angle at C.
typical_uses: Compute lengths and characterize right angles via the converse.
common_misuses: Applying it to a non-right triangle.
repair_templates: Verify which side is the hypotenuse and where the right angle lies.

source: Geometry_ Euclid and Beyond.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Power of a point
statement: For secants through a point P meeting a circle at A,B and C,D, PA times PB equals PC times PD; for a tangent PT, PT squared equals PA times PB.
conditions: The indicated lines and circle intersections are defined.
conclusion: The product of directed distances from P to the two intersection points is invariant.
common_misuses: Ignoring directed lengths or using an external/interior point inconsistently.
bridge_lemmas: Similar triangles formed by intersecting chords.
repair_templates: Choose a consistent orientation for all directed segments.

source: Geometry_ Euclid and Beyond.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Radical axis theorem
statement: The locus of points with equal powers with respect to two nonconcentric circles is a line perpendicular to the line of centers; radical axes of three circles concur or are parallel.
conditions: The circles are distinct and their power functions are defined.
conclusion: Equal-power loci are linear and satisfy the radical-center relation.
typical_uses: Locate common chord lines and prove concurrency.
common_misuses: Treating coincident circles as having a unique radical axis.
bridge_lemmas: Subtract the two circle equations to obtain a linear equation.
repair_templates: Handle concentric or coincident exceptional cases separately.

source: Geometry_ Euclid and Beyond.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Inversion maps circles and lines
statement: Inversion about a circle maps circles through the center to lines avoiding the center and maps other circles to circles; it preserves angles up to orientation.
conditions: A nonzero inversion center and radius are fixed.
conclusion: Incidence and angle calculations can be transported through inversion.
typical_uses: Transform difficult circle configurations into line configurations.
common_misuses: Forgetting that circles through the inversion center become lines.
bridge_lemmas: OP times OP' equals inversion radius squared.
repair_templates: Classify each object by whether it passes through the inversion center.

source: Geometry_ Euclid and Beyond.pdf; rewritten seed rule
name: Euler characteristic for convex polyhedra
statement: For a convex polyhedron, V-E+F=2, where V,E,F count vertices, edges, and faces.
conditions: The polyhedron is finite and topologically a sphere.
conclusion: The combinatorial counts satisfy Euler's relation.
common_misuses: Applying the formula to higher-genus or self-intersecting complexes without correction.
bridge_lemmas: Induction by removing a face or planar graph Euler formula.
repair_templates: Check the underlying cell decomposition is spherical.
